name: Exon Inclusion (Splice Correction)
therapeuticGoalDescription: Restore production of a functional protein by promoting inclusion of a therapeutically important exon during pre-mRNA splicing.
molecularDefect: Diseases caused by exon skipping or defective exon recognition, where inclusion of the skipped exon restores production of a functional transcript.
diseaseMechanism: Steric-blocking ASOs bind splice-silencing elements or inhibitory splice-regulatory sequences, preventing binding of negative splicing factors and promoting exon recognition by the spliceosome.
suitableVariantTypes: Splice-site variants; intronic variants disrupting normal splicing; exon-skipping mutations; selected deep intronic variants where exon inclusion restores function.
typicalDiseases: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMN2 exon 7 inclusion); Pompe disease (investigational); selected inherited metabolic and neurological disorders under investigation.
rnaTargetRegion: Intronic splicing silencers (ISS); exonic splicing silencers (ESS); splice donor/acceptor regulatory regions adjacent to the target exon.
transcriptRequirement: A transcript in which restoring inclusion of the target exon increases production of a functional protein.
asoChemistry: RNase H-independent steric-blocking ASOs. Clinically validated chemistries include 2′-O-methoxyethyl phosphorothioate (2′-MOE PS) (e.g., nusinersen); PMO and other steric-blocking chemistries are also used experimentally.
typicalLength: Approximately 18–25 nucleotides, depending on target and chemistry.
designRules: Literature synthesis: target validated splice-silencing elements; avoid RNase H-active chemistries; experimentally verify exon inclusion by RT-PCR and protein restoration assays.
secondaryStructureRequirement: Accessible splice-regulatory regions within the pre-mRNA are preferred to maximize ASO binding and splice correction.
offTargetConsiderations: Potential unintended modulation of alternative splicing in partially complementary transcripts; transcriptome-wide splice analysis is recommended.
advantages: Clinically validated mechanism; restores endogenous protein expression; reversible and sequence-specific; does not require genome editing.
limitations: Applicable only when exon inclusion restores protein function; repeated dosing required; efficacy depends on target accessibility and splice biology.
clinicalTrialExamples: Spinraza (nusinersen); investigational exon-inclusion ASOs for Pompe disease and other rare genetic disorders.

evidenceLevel.note: FDA-approved therapy with extensive clinical validation.

referencesSummary: Hua et al. (2010); Chen et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2024); FDA prescribing information for Spinraza.

references.paper: Hua Y. et al. Antisense correction of SMN2 splicing in the CNS rescues necrosis in SMA mice. Nature (2010)
references.usedFor: Foundational demonstration of exon inclusion in SMA.
